sections.content: [Placeholder passage text about tunnels: qanat method used in Persia — sloped underground channel to direct tunnelling/water flow; water runs into a cistern/well/pool used by local people; vertical shafts for removing earth and for ventilation. Counter-excavation method: developed later (6th century BCE but did NOT completely replace qanat); required skilled builders. Saldae aqueduct: information found on an inscription/stone tablet (not a book); the two tunnel halves failed to meet (TRUE). Dolaucothi mines in Wales extracted gold. Tunnels could have names of patron and architect carved on them. Cevlik tunnel at Seleuceia Pieria built to protect the harbour/port.]

sections.content: [Placeholder passage text about digital reading vs print reading: technology has a hidden effect on us (reading habits). Sherry Turkle says we should be aware of what is lost when innovation occurs. Brain circuits adjust to whatever is required of them (not that reading is an inborn ability). Mark Edmundson says college students' attitudes don't match those of the general public. Studies: Mangen — students read print vs digital, question-and-answer technique to test comprehension; screen readers found order of information hard to recall. Ziming Liu — students reading isolated words/phrases to save time; gives superficial understanding of emotional content. Writer's views: medium affects choice of content; all age groups at risk; no mention of false information; we still have opportunities to rectify the problems.]

content: There have been many studies on digital screen use, showing some
trends. Psychologist Anne Mangen gave high-school students a short story to read, half using digital and half using print mediums. Her team then used a question-and-answer technique to find out how
each group's understanding of the plot was. The findings showed a clear pattern in the responses, with those who read screens finding the order of information

to recall.

Studies by Ziming Liu show that students are tending to read
words and phrases in a text to save time. This approach, she says, gives the reader a superficial understanding of the
content of material, leaving no time for thought.
